title: The 1968 NATO Conference and the Deliberate Choice of 'Engineering'
explainer: In October 1968, NATO convened computer scientists and practitioners in Garmisch, Germany, under the title "Software Engineering" - a label chosen somewhat provocatively, since at the time most people treated writing programs as a craft, not an engineering discipline. The conference was organized as a response to what attendees called the "software crisis": large projects that ran over budget and schedule because they were managed like craft work rather than with the specifications, estimation, and quality control of engineering. The name stuck because it posed exactly the question this lesson asks: what does it mean to treat building software as an engineering discipline rather than just writing code?

title: Fred Brooks's The Mythical Man-Month (1975)
explainer: Drawing on his experience managing IBM's OS/360 operating-system project, Fred Brooks argued in his 1975 book that the hard part of large software projects is not writing code but coordinating people: communication overhead grows faster than team size, which is why "adding manpower to a late software project makes it later," now known as Brooks's law. It's one of the clearest illustrations of why software engineering is treated as its own discipline distinct from programming - estimation, team structure, and coordination are problems that simply don't exist when one person codes alone.
